title: The four Sunan
hookLine: Abu Dawud, Tirmidhi, Nasa'i, Ibn Majah complete the six books

cards: Smiling in your brother's face is charity. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ said that, in a report from a book we haven't opened yet: the collection of al-Tirmidhi. The two Sahihs aren't the whole shelf.
Beside them stand four more books, and together the six make up a set known as the six books: al-Bukhari, Muslim, and four collections with a plainer name. Today, the four Sunan.

teach.b: First, the word. Sunan is the plural of sunnah: ways, practices. These books are laid out like a handbook of daily life.
Purity, prayer, charity, fasting, trade, marriage, food. Want to know what the Prophet did about something practical? Open a Sunan to that chapter and start reading.
Second, the names. Four compilers, each known by a short name: Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, and Ibn Majah.

teach.h: A ROLL CALL OF FOUR NAMES.
teach.b: Say them like a roll call. Each book has its own habits. Al-Tirmidhi we met a week ago, stepping out after a report to give his verdict on it.
He often also names which scholars acted on it. Third, the honest part.
Sunan doesn't mean sahih. These books hold reports graded sound, reports graded good, and some graded weak, and the compilers often say so themselves.
That's why this path spent days on grading before it reached the books. A hadith's book tells you where it's kept. Its grade tells you how firm it is.
You want both. Fourth, the set. Al-Bukhari and Muslim, plus these four, are called the six books, al-kutub al-sitta.

teach.h: THE SIXTH SEAT WAS ARGUED OVER.
teach.b: Scholars didn't all agree on who belongs in the sixth seat; some placed Malik's Muwatta there instead of Ibn Majah, and tomorrow we meet Malik himself.
Next time you see a hadith cited with a book name and a number, you may recognize the name.

how: Students of hadith learn the six books by name, and when a hadith is cited from one of the Sunan, a careful teacher checks its grade as well as its source.

practice: Count the six on your fingers, one name for each breath: on one hand, al-Bukhari and Muslim, the two Sahihs; on the other, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah. Say them once more without looking at your hands.
Then let the names rest, and keep one line from al-Tirmidhi's book: a smile in your brother's face is charity.
